lessons.title: Shares, Stock Exchanges and What a Share Price Really Tells You

children.text: Share prices are quoted everywhere and explained almost nowhere. This lesson covers what a share actually is, how a price gets set on NSE and BSE, and what that number does and does not tell you about the company behind it.
What You Actually Own

markDefs.definition: A unit of ownership in a company. Owning shares makes you a part owner of the business, with a claim on whatever is left after all obligations are met.
The nominal value printed on a share, used for accounting and corporate actions. It has almost no connection to what the share trades at in the market.
The right to whatever remains after employees, suppliers, lenders and tax authorities have been paid. Shareholders are last in line, which is why equity is riskier than debt.

children.text: A
share

is a unit of ownership in a company, not a lottery ticket and not a loan. If a company has 10 crore shares outstanding and you own 500 of them, you own 0.00005% of that business: its factories, its brand, its cash and its problems. What you hold is a
residual claim
, which is why the
face value
printed on the share, often ₹1, ₹2, ₹5 or ₹10, tells you nothing about what the share is worth.

body.label: Face Value vs Market Price
body.context: A share with a face value of ₹5 may trade at ₹50 or ₹5,000. Face value matters for dividends declared as a percentage, splits and bonus issues, not for valuation.

body.title: Shareholder vs Lender: Two Very Different Deals

columns.label: If You Own Shares (Equity)
points: You are an owner, with voting rights on major decisions
You get paid last, only after lenders, staff, suppliers and tax
Your return is unlimited on the upside and can fall to zero
Dividends are optional and can be skipped in a bad year
You benefit fully when the business does better than expected

columns.label: If You Lend (Debt)
points: You are a creditor, with no say in running the business
You get paid before shareholders, and can enforce your claim
Your return is capped at the agreed interest rate
Interest is a contractual obligation, not a choice
You gain nothing extra if the business does spectacularly well

body.caption: What a Share Entitles You To

cells: Dividends when the board declares them, paid per share held
One vote per share on resolutions, usually exercised electronically before the AGM
A share of whatever is left if the company is wound up, after every other claim is settled
Entitlement to bonus shares, stock splits, rights issues and buyback offers
Quarterly results, annual reports and material disclosures, which listed companies must file with the exchanges

body.title: Last in Line
body.question: A listed company is wound up. Its assets are sold, raising less than the total of what it owes. Who gets paid before shareholders?
options: Nobody, since shareholders are the owners
Only the banks that lent to the company
Employees, suppliers, lenders and tax authorities
body.explanation: Shareholders hold a residual claim, which means they receive whatever is left after every other claim is met. In most failed companies there is nothing left, which is exactly why equity carries higher risk and, in exchange, higher potential return than lending.

children.text: Where the Price Comes From: The Order Book

Nobody sets the share price. It emerges from an order book, a live queue of buy and sell orders at different prices. Buyers post the highest price they will pay, sellers post the lowest they will accept, and a trade happens whenever the two meet.

markDefs.definition: The gap between the highest price a buyer is willing to pay (the bid) and the lowest price a seller will accept (the ask). A narrow spread signals a liquid, actively traded stock.

children.text: The highest bid here is ₹512.30 and the lowest ask is ₹512.45. Nothing trades until somebody crosses that gap, called the
bid-ask spread

. In a Nifty 50 stock the spread is usually a few paise, because thousands of participants are queued up. In a thinly traded small company it can be several rupees wide, which is a cost you pay the moment you transact.

body.title: Read the Spread
body.prompt: Using the order book above, what is the bid-ask spread in rupees?
body.explanation: ₹512.45 minus ₹512.30 equals ₹0.15. If you buy at the ask and immediately sell at the bid, you lose that ₹0.15 per share before any brokerage or taxes. On 1,000 shares that is ₹150, which is why spread matters more than most beginners assume.

body.text: The price you see quoted is the last traded price, the price at which the most recent trade happened. It reflects the opinion of the last two people who transacted, not a valuation of the company's assets and not a promise about tomorrow.

children.text: Over a single day those trades get summarised into four numbers: the opening price, the highest and lowest price of the day, and the closing price. That is all a candlestick chart is showing you.

body.title: One Week of Trading in a Sample Stock (Illustrative)

children.text: What the Price Is Really Telling You

A share price on its own is meaningless. A ₹50 share is not cheap and a ₹5,000 share is not expensive, because price depends on how many shares the company chose to split its ownership into. Two numbers make it meaningful.

body.caption: What the market says the whole company is worth, which is the number to compare across companies.
How many rupees the market is paying for each rupee of annual profit.

children.text: Take a company with 10 crore shares outstanding, a share price of ₹600 and earnings per share of ₹20.

stats.label: Share Price
stats.context: The last traded price on NSE

stats.label: Earnings per Share
stats.context: Annual profit divided by shares outstanding

stats.label: P/E Ratio
stats.context: ₹600 ÷ ₹20, so investors pay ₹30 for every ₹1 of annual profit

children.text: A P/E of 30 is the market saying it expects profits to grow. Nobody pays 30 years of current profit for a business they expect to stand still. This is the single most important idea in the lesson: the share price is a bet on the future, not a report card on the past.

body.text: A share price is not a measure of how the company performed. It is a measure of how the company performed against what the market already expected. Good results with weak guidance can still send the stock down.

body.title: Price Moves More Than Profit Does (Illustrative Five Years)

children.text: Earnings per share doubled over those five years, from ₹12 to ₹24. The share price tripled, from ₹240 to ₹720. The extra move came from the P/E rising from 20 to 30, which is the market becoming more optimistic. When sentiment turns, that same multiple can compress just as fast, with profits unchanged.

body.title: Why Two Companies With Identical Profits Trade at Different Prices

children.text: Two companies each earn ₹100 crore a year. One trades at 15 times earnings, the other at 45. The market is not being irrational. It is pricing four things:
Growth.
Profit expected to grow 25% a year is worth far more than the same profit expected to stay flat.
Predictability.
A consumer company selling soap every month earns steadier profits than a commodity producer whose earnings swing with global prices.
Capital needed to grow.
A software firm can double revenue without building a plant. A steel maker cannot.
Trust.
Governance history, related party dealings and disclosure quality all show up in the multiple investors are willing to pay.

body.title: "The Company Lost ₹600 Crore Today"
body.scenario: You work in internal communications at a listed company. A business channel reports that the company "lost ₹600 crore in market capitalisation" after the share price fell from ₹600 to ₹540. The company has 10 crore shares outstanding. Two department heads forward the clip asking whether budgets are about to be cut.
body.prompt: Is the company ₹600 crore poorer? What is the accurate way to describe what happened?
body.modelAnswer: No. Market capitalisation fell from ₹6,000 crore to ₹5,400 crore, a drop of ₹600 crore, but that is a change in what investors collectively think the business is worth, not money leaving the company's bank account. Not a rupee moved out of the company: the shares changed hands between investors in the secondary market, so the loss sits with shareholders who now hold shares worth less than before. The company's cash balance, order book and payroll capacity are exactly what they were yesterday. Budgets are decided by the company's cash flows and plans, not by a one-day price move. The honest caveat is that a sustained fall does matter, because it makes future fundraising costlier, reduces the value of employee stock options and often reflects genuine concerns investors have about the outlook. So the accurate line is: shareholders are poorer today, the company is not, and if the fall persists it will eventually affect what the company can afford to do.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: Share price multiplied by the number of shares outstanding gives a company's market ___.
body.explanation: Market capitalisation is the number to compare across companies, never the share price on its own. A ₹50 share can belong to a far larger company than a ₹5,000 share, depending on how many shares each has issued.

body.title: Look Up Your Own Employer or a Major Customer
steps: Find the company on screener.in and note its market capitalisation, not just its share price
Note the P/E ratio and compare it with two competitors in the same industry
Check the face value, and see for yourself how little it has to do with the market price
Open the latest quarterly results and find earnings per share, then divide the price by it to confirm the P/E yourself
Look at the five-year chart of sales and profit, and ask whether the price trend is explained by the business or by changing sentiment

body.label: screener.in
body.description: Free access to Indian listed company financials: market cap, P/E, quarterly results and ten-year history on one page. The fastest way to check any claim made in a meeting about a listed company.

points: A share is a unit of ownership carrying a residual claim, which is paid only after employees, suppliers, lenders and tax authorities
Face value is an accounting number and says nothing about what a share is worth
Prices are set by an order book of competing bids and asks, and the quoted price is simply the last trade that happened
The bid-ask spread is a real cost, narrow in liquid Nifty 50 stocks and wide in thinly traded ones
Share price alone means nothing; market capitalisation tells you company size and the P/E ratio tells you what the market is paying per rupee of profit
Prices move on expectations, not on results alone, which is why a company can report higher profit and still see its stock fall
A fall in market capitalisation is a loss to shareholders, not cash leaving the company
